stories.headline: Cornell rape case: Hochul proposes rape law changes, accuser's lawyer says she is 'under siege'

spectrum.tilt_pill: Coverage is balanced across the spectrum

claims.text: The accuser, identified as Jane Doe, alleges she was drugged and raped by several men—dubbed the 'Cornell Seven'—at a Cornell University fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, in 2024.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten's office initially declined to file charges, saying the evidence did not meet the legal threshold at the time.
Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University on September 16, which brought the case national attention and led to the criminal investigation being reopened.
On Friday, Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to lead the case, saying she had 'lost faith' in the county prosecutor's handling of it.
Hochul said she would support a pending state bill to close a legal 'loophole' that makes it difficult to prosecute rape cases when the victim voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol.
The bill to close the loophole was first sponsored by Assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz in 2019.
Jane Doe's lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, said she is 'under siege' on social media from people trying to identify her, including false identifications.
A U.S. Marine Corps sergeant with the same name as one of the accused men was mistakenly served the lawsuit and received threats.
Cornell students held a campus assembly voicing anger over the case.
A 'Justice for Survivors' protest is planned for October 5 calling for expulsions, policy changes, and an external investigation.
Cornell University says it conducted an 'extensive investigation' that resulted in sanctions including expulsions and suspensions.
Cornell University says it is legally barred from disclosing specific disciplinary outcomes.

The case centers on an alleged 2024 gang rape at a Cornell fraternity that went uncharged until a civil lawsuit filed in September 2025 renewed scrutiny of how campus and local officials handled the investigation.

The controversy has intersected with a long-running policy debate in New York over whether rape laws adequately cover cases where a victim voluntarily consumed drugs or alcohol before being assaulted.
Advocates and lawmakers like Assemblyman Dinowitz have sought to address the issue of rape laws covering voluntary intoxication since 2019.
The episode has drawn broader attention to fraternity culture and university accountability.
The episode has drawn broader attention to the risks faced by anonymous accusers when cases attract intense online scrutiny.
The case highlights a genuine tension between protecting an alleged survivor's safety and anonymity and ensuring fair process for accused individuals who have not been charged.
The tension is underscored by both the online efforts to identify Jane Doe and the public naming of the accused men.
The case will likely continue to shape New York's legislative debate over intoxication and consent laws.
The bill to close the loophole may potentially advance when the legislature reconvenes in January or sooner if Hochul calls a special session.
Attorney General James's takeover of the investigation could determine whether criminal charges are eventually filed.
Cornell faces ongoing pressure from students and advocates over campus safety policies and fraternity oversight.

stories.headline: Russia strikes second major bridge in Kyiv, killing at least five across Ukraine and Russia
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on AP
body: A Russian strike hit a second major bridge in Kyiv on Saturday, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said, as Moscow intensified attacks on critical infrastructure in Ukraine's capital. The attack on the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge injured two people and damaged the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires, causing traffic jams, Klitschko said. It came after the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones this week, with Klitschko warning that "the enemy is tearing Kyiv apart."

At least five people were killed in a series of long-range strikes carried out by Kyiv and Moscow on Saturday. In Ukraine's Odesa region, a Russian attack on a Liberia-flagged civilian ship killed one sailor and injured three others, the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority said. Twelve other crew members were safely evacuated. Two people were reportedly killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russia-occupied Luhansk region, according to the Moscow-installed governor. In the occupied Zaporizhia region, Russian-installed authorities said one person was killed and 10 others injured in a Ukrainian drone attack. Russian media also reported one person killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Belgorod region. At least 12 people were injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv and Kyiv regions, local officials said.

The two Kyiv bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday. The strikes have severed road, rail and trolleybus links across the river. The ongoing drone threat means restrictions on other routes, bringing traffic jams to the city's roads for a second day, though Friday's gridlock has not been repeated to the same level. Many of the city's three million residents rely on the metro to travel across the city daily. The fear is this new Russian tactic will result in sustained attacks which could effectively cut the city in two.

Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. Moscow again urged foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv. Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges, but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable. More powerful weapons could collapse the bridges, some of which are reported to be in poor condition after years carrying heavier traffic than they were designed for. Ukrainian lawmakers discussed the state of Kyiv's bridges in a recent meeting, setting out contingency plans to use ferries or temporary pontoon bridges to keep the city connected in the event of any bridges being destroyed.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Putin had decided that there were "no rules now" when attacking Ukraine. In an interview with the Financial Times, he said: "The Russians have failed to occupy us. So now they are carrying out massive attacks and mass killings." He added: "They want to destroy our bridges... our data centres, the internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, universities - everything. They want people to flee their cities." Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday insisted that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian economic targets were a direct response to Ukraine's strikes on Russia's oil refineries and its ships in the Black Sea. "Now from every direction we're receiving calls 'let's stop'. But they started it," Putin said after a wide-ranging speech at the Valdai foreign policy forum. The Kremlin leader admitted Kyiv had "got some results" from its refinery attacks and Russia had lost about 1% of its GDP. Ukraine maintains it began attacking Russian oil infrastructure because it helps the Kremlin finance the war.

Russia has targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in February 2022. Russia's all-out war on Ukraine is in its fifth year and shows little sign of slowing down. Russian battlefield gains have slowed to a near-record low, with Ukrainian counterattacks, including one ongoing push around the town of Lyman in the east, mitigating Russian territorial gains elsewhere. Russia has increased its attacks on civilian infrastructure in recent months, including with the growing use of jet-powered long-range strike drones, which move faster and are harder to shoot down. Ukraine has also engaged in significant long-range strikes, including targeting Russian oil infrastructure and military-industrial facilities deep inside Russian territory.

stories.headline: Brazil votes Sunday in high-stakes presidential rematch between Lula and Bolsonaro's son
body: Brazilians vote Sunday in a presidential election that pits 80-year-old leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro — a rematch of the bitter 2022 contest with outsized stakes for Brazil and for Latin America's political alignment. Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race; if no candidate wins more than 50% of valid votes, the top two finishers will meet in an Oct. 25 runoff. Brazil uses electronic voting machines and typically counts results within hours, so it should be clear by Sunday night whether a runoff is coming.

The younger Bolsonaro is carrying his father's political movement. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup to overturn his 2022 loss to Lula — a scheme that included a plan to assassinate Lula, according to police — and is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup. Flávio has promised to pardon his father if elected, has voiced few policy differences from him, has cast doubt on humans' responsibility for climate change, and supports making it easier for Brazilians to buy guns. He has pledged to join the US-led Shield of the Americas coalition and follow an 'iron fist' approach to crime. Bolsonaro's only previous bid for executive office ended in fourth place in Rio's 2016 mayoral race, but analysts say he has emerged as a serious challenger partly through a transfer of his father's voter base and partly through anti-Lula sentiment.

Lula is seeking a fourth term. His campaign has been hit by corruption allegations — still under investigation — involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving Supreme Court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president. Voters also worry about insecurity, corruption and the economy. Lula's public-spending push drove early growth, but growth has since slowed; Bolsonaro argues Brazil's hefty national debt is holding back the economy, and a top adviser has pledged to reduce it by slashing spending along the lines of Argentina's Javier Milei. Lula banned online betting days before the vote, while unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen and average incomes have risen under his watch. Bolsonaro also took money from a jailed ex-banker known for bribery and is being investigated on money-laundering charges, which he denies.

The next president will nominate four of 11 Supreme Court justices, giving the winner significant influence over the court for years, and will shape Brazil's economy, environmental policy, relationship with the United States, and the future of its young democracy. Trump looms large: Rallies for Flávio have featured US flags, and Washington imposed privileged access to Brazil's rare earths and critical minerals as a condition for not applying tariffs — which Lula rejected, while Bolsonaro has offered those resources to help the US 'break its dependence on China.' Lula has raised sovereignty concerns about Trump's 'war on drugs' — used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations with US military personnel — and has accused Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro's favor, joined by Democratic members of the US Congress.

Analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still able to say 'no' to Trump's whims. 'Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,' said Pedro Telles of Brazil's FGV university. 'But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally.' A Bolsonaro victory would be used 'triumphantly' by Trump to produce an 'almost completely aligned region,' said Georgetown University's Michael Shifter, who added that 'democracy is also kind of on the line here' — noting Flávio is only running because his father cannot. 'Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region's autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,' said Sandra Borda Guzmán of Colombia's Universidad de los Andes.

Voters are polarized. Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, said she will vote for Flávio even though her first choice, far-right former governor Ronaldo Caiado, polls at 4%: 'Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I'm going with Flávio so we can get Lula out.' Actor Docy Moreira, 59, who moved 1,550 miles to escape Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 victory, will vote for Lula. Most of her family will back the son. 'If not, it will be devastating, but I'm not going to move again. I'm stronger now. I've learned that I can find refuge within myself,' she said.

The election will also test the reach of the pro-Trump bloc. Trump has boasted that every rightwing candidate he endorsed has won the seven presidential elections held in the region since his second term began, leaving only a handful of leftwing governments — Brazil and Mexico among them — outside the Shield of the Americas, a 15-nation anti-drug cartel coalition. At the coalition's latest meeting, Trump referenced Latin America's 'tremendous natural wealth,' widely read as a warning against China. Federal and state legislative seats and governorships are also on Sunday's ballot, with a runoff for president or governor on Oct. 25 if needed.

stories.headline: Flydubai co-pilot used axe in cockpit attack, identified as Hamam al-Hammami
body: The co-pilot of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv attacked the captain with a crash axe and tried to take control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general said, as the plane carrying more than 170 people plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey. Passengers overpowered the attacker, and two reserve pilots safely landed the plane in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. The co-pilot has been identified by multiple media outlets as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national, though there has been no official confirmation.

Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was stabbed in the attack. He later described lying injured on the cockpit floor as the aircraft descended. 'When I was down, I could feel that the aircraft was plummeting, and I knew this is the last chance to do something,' he told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. 'I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside.' Once the door was opened, passengers rushed to help. An Israeli woman, Tali Manes, had raised the alarm after hearing a commotion from the cockpit. Her husband, Zvika, along with three other men—Yaniv Hayun, Dr Shota Musayev and Asaf Rajuan—entered the cockpit. Hayun described putting the attacker in a chokehold and pulling him out, then pulling the plane's controls. The aircraft had first signalled a general emergency (squawk 7700) before switching to squawk 7500, the code for unlawful interference or hijacking.

Al-Hammami's background has come under scrutiny. According to reports, Omani authorities had previously barred him from flying over concerns about alleged extremist views, and he was removed from flight training at Oman Air before being reassigned. He completed a three-year distance-learning course in aviation management at Buckinghamshire New University in the UK, graduating in 2023; the university said he did not undertake any pilot training there.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News that after being subdued, the attacker 'calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal—that's not a question.' Netanyahu added that the attacker 'underwent Islamist radical indoctrination' and that the stabbed pilot and passengers 'managed to prevent a 9/11 disaster'. The UAE has begun investigating whether the incident was linked to terrorist activity. Machchhar, who was airlifted to Abu Dhabi, is reported to be in stable condition. 'I am not looking at this wound like a wound because that would make my recovery even more difficult,' he said. 'I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again.'

stories.headline: Ethiopian government forces retake Tigray airport as rebels retreat from Mekelle
body: Ethiopia’s federal army and pro-government fighters have recaptured the main airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, with Tigrayan rebels seen retreating from the city, multiple unnamed sources told Reuters and AFP on Saturday. The Alula Aba Noga Airport, about 10km (6 miles) east of the city centre, was one of three airfields seized by rebel forces at the start of the fighting on September 23. A local journalist told AFP that TPLF militants and leaders were leaving Mekelle, though federal forces had not yet been seen inside the city. Residents expressed fears of looting and lawlessness, with one saying, 'I am worried that lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life.'

The fighting, which erupted last week between Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies, has shattered the fragile Pretoria Agreement peace deal signed in November 2022. The conflict has spread across multiple fronts in Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions. In Amhara’s North Wollo area, the Ethiopian military reported about 270 Tigrayan fighters killed and more than 200 wounded. The Tigray Peace Force, an armed group aligned with the federal government, captured the town of Alamata near Tigray’s southern border, a key supply hub. Fighting in Afar threatens supply routes from Djibouti, through which most Ethiopian imports pass. Outside the north, an explosion was reported early Thursday at the Ministry of Defence in Addis Ababa, marking an apparent spillover into the capital.

The humanitarian toll is mounting. At least 52 civilians have been killed, and Doctors Without Borders (MSF) reported a surge in wounded in the north. Amnesty International said on Friday it had received 'credible reports of destruction of civilian objects through shelling and air strikes, intensified forced conscription, and other acts that may constitute violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law.' Amnesty’s regional director for East and Southern Africa, Tigere Chagutah, urged the African Union’s Peace and Security Council to 'urgently convene an emergency session on the situation in Ethiopia,' warning that 'fears of regionalisation of the conflict are on the rise.'

TPLF leader Debretsion Gebremichael said in a video that 'the war is regional and it is a war to control the Red Sea.' Analysts fear the fighting could draw in neighbouring countries, with Laura Hammond of SOAS University of London telling Al Jazeera that 'the risks that conflict will spread to other countries … are already playing out.' stories.headline: Aaron Judge left off Yankees' ALDS roster due to calf strain
body: New York Yankees slugger Aaron Judge was not included on the team's 26-man roster for the American League Division Series against the Tampa Bay Rays, the club's network first reported, due to a right calf strain that may threaten his availability for the remainder of October. Judge, 34, suffered the injury on Sept. 16 at Minnesota, just seven games after returning from a rib fracture. He played in only 66 games this season after winning consecutive AL MVP awards.

Judge sat out the Yankees' two-game sweep of the Boston Red Sox in the AL Wild Card round. Before that series, he took simulated at-bats at the team's Class AAA facility in Somerset. After the Yankees flew to Tampa for the ALDS, he worked out at their spring training facility and also went through the off-day workout at Tropicana Field. Manager Aaron Boone did not specify whether Judge had run the bases in his rehab progression, often one of the final steps to a return, but noted he had tested the calf in other ways. Judge had vowed to "do all he can" to play against the Rays.

On Monday, Judge took live batting practice at Yankee Stadium and took more live at-bats at the team's Double-A affiliate in Somerset on Wednesday. He told reporters he had been limited in his activities. Boone said on Wednesday, "We feel like in a couple weeks since the injury, he's made real strides and significant improvements. Hopefully, we're in a position to make another decision in a couple of days."

New York's sweep of Boston marked its first playoff games contested without Judge since 2015. The Rays won the AL East in Judge's absence. The Yankees now open the ALDS in Tampa without their three-time MVP, whose calf strain may threaten his viability for the rest of the postseason.

stories.headline: 49ers Owner Jed York Suspended Six Weeks, Fined $500,000 for Prostitution Arrest
body: The NFL announced Friday that San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York has been suspended from attending six games and fined $500,000 for violating the league’s personal conduct policy, stemming from his arrest in an Ohio prostitution sting in August. The suspension was reported by Mike Garafolo of NFL Network.

York, 46, was arrested in East Palestine, Ohio, on suspicion of engaging in prostitution. Prosecutors later amended the charges to disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools, to which York pleaded no contest. The league’s statement noted that York has already stayed away from San Francisco’s first three games of the season, which will count toward his suspension. He will be eligible to resume attending games after Tuesday, October 20.

In a statement released Friday, York said: “Today, the NFL concluded its review, and I accept its decision in full. To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry. This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one’s failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better. Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don’t take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead.”

York joined the 49ers in 2005 as director of strategic planning for his family-owned team. He was promoted to vice president of strategic planning before becoming CEO in December 2008, when his parents transitioned to co-chairmen. He currently serves as principal owner and CEO, a role he has held since 2024. During his 17 years as CEO, the 49ers have posted a 147-129-1 record with eight playoff appearances and three Super Bowl appearances.

stories.headline: Verstappen Takes First 2026 Pole in Bahrain; Red Bull Upgrade Praised
body: Max Verstappen secured his and Red Bull's first pole position of the 2026 Formula 1 season with a dominant qualifying performance at the Bahrain Grand Prix, held at the Sepang International Circuit in Malaysia. Verstappen, whose last pole and victory came at the 2025 season finale in Abu Dhabi, topped all three qualifying sessions and posted a fastest lap of 1:35.130, 0.298 seconds ahead of Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton. Red Bull's Isack Hadjar qualified third but will start eighth due to a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his permitted number of engine parts, promoting championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes to third on the grid.

The result marks a significant turnaround for Red Bull, which started the season off the pace—the car was on average more than 0.5 seconds per lap slower than Mercedes in the first half of the year. An aerodynamic upgrade centered on a new floor, introduced at the last race in Azerbaijan, proved transformative at the demanding Sepang track, which features long corners and a rough surface in tropical heat. Verstappen said: 'It's been an incredible result for us. Looking at the season, how it started for us and the progression that we have made. At some tracks we were kind of close, but now I think this weekend it was very positive for us. We have been adding bits to the car and they have worked. It's simple as that.' Team-mate Hadjar, who missed three races after the summer break with a broken wrist sustained while boxing, added: 'I jumped in a car that's way better than when I left it in Budapest. The last two weekends have been surprising.'

Hamilton, starting from his equal best grid position of the year in second, acknowledged the challenge ahead. 'It's so hot here. That's made it a massive challenge for the cars, the tyres, the mechanics in the garage. Because the tyres are sliding, it's so hard to find a good balance and we made one change and we finally hit the sweet spot,' he said. Hamilton added that his mindset for Sunday's race was to 'just try my best to hold on to him tomorrow.' Verstappen has dominated the weekend so far on Formula 1's return to Sepang for the first time since 2017, and the front-row pairing revives memories of their no-holds-barred title battle in 2021.

Mercedes brought their first major aerodynamic upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix in June, but it has not yet delivered the expected step forward. Antonelli, who under-performed slightly in qualifying due to an unusual tyre strategy and a track-limits violation, said: 'With this new package, obviously the window of the way the car operates is different. So, we're trying to understand in which window the car performance is best. Our high-speed performance has been very strong this weekend, but in the low-speed we lacked.' Team-mate George Russell could manage only eighth fastest, 0.741 seconds off the pace, and said: 'It's the most demanding circuit on the tyres, so we don't know exactly why we didn't have the pace. The others have caught up and overtaken [us].' McLaren, tipped by Russell as potential frontrunners, also struggled; Lando Norris was sixth, 0.627 seconds behind.

The race on Sunday is expected to be dominated by tyre degradation in stifling heat, with the possibility of rain. Antonelli noted that track position and strategy will be critical, saying: 'Tomorrow might be two stops, three stops. We don't know. But the only thing we know is that it's going to be roasting hot out there.' Elsewhere, Fernando Alonso, who recently confirmed he will stay in F1 for at least another year in 2027, gave Aston Martin their best qualifying of the year with 12th place, 1.524 seconds off the pace. Alonso said: 'It was definitely one of the best qualifying of the year. It seems this circuit is a little better for our package and let's see tomorrow if we can take advantage of this.'

Off the track, a separate controversy emerged over driver cooling vests. Mercedes opted not to use the FIA-approved active cooling gear at the Bahrain Grand Prix to stay under the budget cap, and Russell described driving the upgraded W17 in the 60°C Sepang heat as 'sitting in an oven.' Verstappen, who has routinely refused to use the system and previously called the mandatory heat-emergency components 'ridiculous,' dismissed Russell's complaints. 'You shouldn't make a fuss,' Verstappen said, suggesting the issue is one of physical conditioning rather than a financial or engineering problem.

stories.headline: Man City whistleblower loses witness protection; trail of inflated transfers examined
body: The Portuguese computer hacker who leaked documents that triggered the Premier League investigation into Manchester City is set to lose his witness protection, despite his fears of assassination. Rui Pinto, founder of Football Leaks, posted on X that the decision to terminate his participation in the programme on 10 October has put him in a 'life-threatening situation,' leaving him no alternative but to relocate to an undisclosed location because of 'multiple death threats' and 'the serious risk of an assassination attempt.' Pinto, 37, was convicted in Portugal of illegal access to data and attempted extortion and given a four-year suspended sentence; he wore a bulletproof vest during his first trial in 2020.

Pinto released a tranche of confidential football documents in 2018, including emails and financial records relating to Manchester City, which were shared with German magazine Der Spiegel and used for investigations into the club's finances and alleged breaches of financial fair play rules. Last week, an independent commission found City guilty of all charges relating to breaches of the Premier League's financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons, a verdict the club has appealed. Pinto's lawyers said the end of his witness protection leaves him at heightened risk, noting legal proceedings from the leaks, including the case against City, remain ongoing. Pinto has set up a fundraising page to help him 'survive this serious situation,' which he claims was 'created by the Portuguese State.'

The commission found that City had 'inflated' its accounts by more than £900m during the period under scrutiny. The club spent roughly £1.2bn on players between 2009 and 2018 (about £900m net spend), more than any other club in that time. That outlay was vital to City becoming England's most successful club and would have been heavily reduced had they not knowingly broken the rules, the commission concluded. The money flowed to 46 different clubs across 19 national league systems. Just over a quarter of City's total transfer outlay went to Premier League clubs; they also paid significant sums to clubs in La Liga, the Bundesliga, Ligue 1, and the Portuguese league.

Among the clubs receiving the highest fees from City were Wolfsburg (for Kevin de Bruyne), Monaco (for Benjamin Mendy and Bernardo Silva), and Arsenal (from whom City bought four players, the most of any club). For some clubs, the fees were the highest they had ever received at the time. However, the money did not always work out beneficially: Wolfsburg dropped from second to eighth in the Bundesliga after losing De Bruyne, and Monaco went from winning Ligue 1 and reaching the Champions League semi-finals to nearly being relegated within two years. Sell-on clauses also funnelled money to clubs not directly involved in the transfers, such as Queens Park Rangers earning roughly £9m from Raheem Sterling's move from Liverpool, and Barnsley taking about £7m from the John Stones transfer.

The independent commission's verdict and the club's appeal have drawn attention to the broader impact of City's spending. The Premier League investigation was triggered by Pinto's leaks, and his loss of witness protection adds a new dimension to the ongoing legal and financial fallout. City have confirmed their appeal against the guilty verdict. Pinto has also turned his attention to FIFA president Gianni Infantino, repeating allegations from 2018 that Infantino intervened to help City and Paris St-Germain avoid UEFA financial fair play sanctions. Infantino's position has recently come under increased pressure following controversial plans to sell stakes in FIFA competitions to private investors.

stories.headline: Congo Ebola outbreak death toll surpasses 4,000 after treatment center burned
stories.byline: Health & Science desk · anchored on AP
body: Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000 people since it was declared in eastern Congo on May 15, the Health Ministry announced Thursday, as the country continues to grapple with the fastest-growing Ebola epidemic in history. The latest figures show 4,018 deaths among 8,300 recorded cases. The outbreak is on track to exceed the deadliest on record — West Africa’s 2014-2016 epidemic, which killed 11,000 people — according to the World Health Organization.

Efforts to contain the virus suffered a setback this week when soldiers searching for weapons burned an Ebola-hit displacement camp that housed a transit center for infected patients in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people to flee. “When we lose a center, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment, and we have to start again,” said Julien Harneis, the U.N. senior Ebola coordinator. “And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need.” Creating such treatment centers has been a struggle, requiring money and staff that are in short supply.

Meanwhile, some health workers at the outbreak’s epicenter in Ituri Province gathered to demand payment for wages owed them. Protesters, including surveillance team members, held placards reading “No money, no data!” and “No payment for months.” Some workers have not been paid for August and September, said Biongi Beiza, a protester in Bunia. “There is no explanation from the administration,” he said. Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hampering containment.

An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders) who was infected with Ebola while working in Congo arrived in the Netherlands late Thursday on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit at Leiden University Medical Center. “The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country,” the group said. At least 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.

Local authorities have deployed mobile laboratories to speed detection. Test results that used to take 72 hours can now be obtained in six hours, said Dr. Lota Kalubi at a treatment center in Butembo. Michel Ngimba of the National Institute of Biomedical Research said the labs can be moved quickly to remote or emergency locations, such as Katwa. The number of newly confirmed cases has fallen — from about 850 cases and 470 deaths per week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September — but Africa CDC said the decline may be due to insecurity and challenges in gaining community cooperation. The virus has accelerated in some areas even as it has slowed in others.

Insecurity and community resistance remain major hurdles. A Congolese politician was beaten to death earlier this week in an emerging hot spot after defending government measures to deal with the outbreak. Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach working with local leaders to educate people about the virus, but those efforts face residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. Deep distrust of the government — over its past handling of Ebola outbreaks and chronic corruption — further complicates the response.

Médecins Sans Frontières said: 'The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country.'
At least 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
Local authorities have deployed mobile laboratories to speed detection.
Test results that used to take 72 hours can now be obtained in six hours, said Dr. Lota Kalubi at a treatment center in Butembo.

The number of newly confirmed cases has fallen from about 850 cases and 470 deaths per week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September.
Africa CDC said the decline may be due to insecurity and challenges in gaining community cooperation.

Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach working with local leaders to educate people about the virus.

stories.headline: Measles outbreaks spread in multiple states; Pennsylvania reports fifth death, New York and Ohio see new cases
body: Measles outbreaks continue to expand across multiple states, with Pennsylvania reporting a fifth death from the disease, according to STAT. The full scope of the outbreak in Pennsylvania and nationwide remains unknown because only confirmed cases are reported; as of Wednesday, the state had 943 confirmed cases, about a quarter of the national total for 2026. Approximately 20% of infected people require hospital care, but some cases never come to the attention of public health authorities, particularly in areas with large Amish populations where vaccination rates are low and medical care may not be sought unless illness becomes severe.

In New York, Lewis County Public Health reported Friday evening that 10 more people had been diagnosed with measles, all unvaccinated. Officials said all 10 cases are linked to a case reported the previous Saturday, which was the first measles case recorded in the county since the state began providing county-by-county data in 1994. Sick residents who are in the infectious period are in isolation and will remain so until they are no longer contagious. Health officials said the overall risk to the public remains low for people fully vaccinated or born before 1957, who are presumed to have natural immunity.

In Ohio, Hancock Public Health confirmed one measles case in Findlay, with the infected individual having visited multiple locations while infectious. Potential exposure sites include NWO Urgent Care on September 29 between 2:30 p.m. and 5:30 p.m., and Blanchard Valley Hospital Emergency Department on the same day between 3:30 p.m. and 6:30 p.m. The agency urged anyone who was at those locations during those times to fill out a close contact investigation form and monitor for symptoms for up to 21 days.

Wisconsin has also seen significant spread, with the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reporting that cases have reached 243 and that the count could be an undercount. Nationwide, the total number of confirmed measles cases stood at 943 in Pennsylvania as of Wednesday, representing about a quarter of the national total for 2026.

Measles is an acute, highly contagious viral disease. Early symptoms typically appear 7 to 14 days after exposure and include high fever (often above 101 degrees F), cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. A red, blotchy rash usually appears 3 to 5 days after initial symptoms, starting on the face and spreading downward. The MMR vaccine given within 72 hours of exposure, or immune globulin given within 6 days, can prevent or reduce severity. Unvaccinated individuals, young infants, pregnant women, and immunocompromised people are at highest risk for severe complications.

"It is much worse than is being claimed," Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, told STAT. "I think we don't know how bad." Health officials urge anyone who develops symptoms to call ahead before seeking medical care and to limit contact with others to prevent further spread.

stories.headline: Trump names Jay Clayton AI czar after 'super intelligence' order
body: The White House this week signed a new executive order rebranding artificial intelligence as "super intelligence" and secured a "morally binding" safety pledge from major tech CEOs.

The executive order, signed September 29, mandates all government agencies to refer to "AI" and "artificial intelligence" as "SI" and "super intelligence," stating that today's frontier systems "do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence" and "increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence." The same week, the White House gathered nearly every major tech CEO — including Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, and Anthropic's Dario Amodei — to sign an AI safety pledge that Trump called "morally binding."

The rebranding has triggered a surge in registrations for the .si domain name, which is associated with Slovenia — First Lady Melania Trump's home country. Registry SI, the official organization managing Slovenia's domains, reported a 2,199% increase in .si domain purchases in September, with 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30 and nearly 13,000 in the past 24 hours. Web hosting platform Hostinger said .si is now its second most popular domain extension, with about 4,300 registered on September 30 and 5,400 on October 1; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in those two days, and more than half the buyers were from the U.S. and India.

Despite the surge, only around 3% of .si domains on Hostinger are explicitly related to AI, with most being "unclassified." Klaudijus Januitis, Hostinger's head of domains, said he expects demand to keep growing but does not see .si replacing .ai anytime soon, calling it a "more affordable second option." On Hostinger, .si costs about $12 a year, while .ai costs $90 with a two-year commitment. "Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw," Januitis said, noting that Anguilla charges a premium for .ai that goes directly to the government, whereas .si fees go to the registry. "For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. For Slovenia, .si is a nice bonus."

Some founders are already buying .si domains to protect their brands or as speculative investments. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, said he bought the .si version of his company name "to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai," adding that "a few founder friends are buying too 'cause we think it's the new AI boom." He noted that domains can be tokenized and traded on the blockchain, though he is unsure if .si is supported yet. "Who knows how far it goes, but I'm happy to take a bet," he said. Meanwhile, Wix said it has not seen a "meaningful uptick" in .si registrations, while GoDaddy does not yet host the .si domain and Squarespace had not responded as of publication.

stories.headline: Apple tightens Mac full-disk access controls over AI agent risks
body: Apple announced Friday that it is introducing new controls for macOS's Full Disk Access permission, citing risks posed by increasingly capable and autonomous AI agents. The change follows a controversy in which Inc. columnist Jason Aten reported that Meta's AI agent Muse had accessed the contents of his private Apple Messages without his explicit permission. Apple said the new controls are designed to ensure that users who wish to grant an app Full Disk Access can do so only with "very explicit user action."

Full Disk Access is a macOS system-level permission that gives an app access to a user's entire system, including files, mail, messages, and browsing history. Apple said the feature was originally designed to allow backup apps to function properly, but that it "largely sidesteps" other privacy controls. In a blog post aimed at developers, Apple stated: "Some developers are using Full Disk Access in ways that could put users at risk, exposing everything on their systems…without users' full knowledge and understanding." The company added: "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially."

The announcement comes two weeks after Aten wrote that Meta's Muse app sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permission to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Meta CTO David Singleton responded that Muse requires two opt-in privileges to access Messages: macOS system-level Full Disk Access and a Messages connector setting within the app. "The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in," Singleton said. "Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled."

Mac security expert Patrick Wardle questioned Singleton's denial, telling Ars Technica: "From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc." When asked how Muse could not read messages when it had Full Disk Access while every other app with that privilege could, Meta PR's only response was to requote Singleton's statement. Meta spokesperson Andy Stone also pushed back on Aten's report, saying access to Messages is "entirely opt-in" and requires enabling both Full Disk Access and the Messages connector.

Apple did not specify when the new controls will roll out. The company did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge or TechCrunch. The decision to tighten Full Disk Access also follows a Wired report that a flaw in ChatGPT's Mac app could have allowed hackers to access sensitive data, according to TechCrunch.

stories.headline: Epic pauses product development to fix security bugs that risk patient data
body: Epic, the software giant behind the widely used MyChart patient portal, has paused most product development for an estimated six weeks to address security vulnerabilities that could expose patient data. CEO Judy Faulkner told Modern Healthcare last month that the pause follows a deployment of Anthropic’s frontier cybersecurity model Mythos, which uncovered flaws that could allow unauthorized access to patients’ medical records.

The company has not disclosed the specific nature of the bugs, but Epic’s chief security officer, Stirling Martin, told The New York Times that certain customer configurations of MyChart could let outsiders view patient records without leaving any trace in the software’s logs. Martin, who did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, told the Times that the AI model did not determine whether the bug could also be used to alter records undetected, but that the risk was serious enough to warrant remediation.

MyChart is used to manage more than 320 million patient records across hospitals and clinics in the United States. Epic says it does not hold customers’ medical data; that responsibility lies with healthcare providers. However, a bug unknown to Epic could potentially allow hackers to compromise multiple MyChart systems nationwide and raid the data stored within.

It is rare for a company to halt product development to fix security bugs, but the emergence of AI tools capable of rapidly finding and exploiting vulnerabilities has heightened concerns about data theft. Healthcare breaches have become increasingly common as attackers target sensitive medical information, often betting that providers will pay ransoms to prevent publication. In 2024, a ransomware attack on Change Healthcare, a UnitedHealth-owned health tech company, exposed data on more than 192 million people—the majority of the U.S. population—and the company paid hackers twice to keep the data private.

This year has already seen a string of healthcare data breaches affecting tens of millions of Americans, including incidents at electronic health data storage firm CareCloud, pharmaceutical distributor McKesson, and U.K.-based health tech company Craneware, whose software is used across North America. The Department of Health and Human Services currently lists a breach at dental insurer DentaQuest affecting 15 million people as the largest healthcare-related data breach of 2026 so far.
